897.title: Rediscovery
897.hook: Western scholars begin reading the Pali texts, and a society forms to print them
897.howItsDone: Buddhist monks and lay readers chant and study the same verses for years, and many now read them alongside older and newer English translations, comparing how each one renders a line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dharmapala, the Sri Lankan layman who campaigned for Bodh Gaya and stood up to speak in Chicago. Your line was he spoke up. Did you say the thing you meant to say? Today, people far away start listening. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

A palm-leaf manuscript, its edges dark from handling, lies open on a table in a European library. The script is one the reader is still learning. For the monks who copied it in Sri Lanka or Burma, these words were nothing new. They had been chanted, taught and copied long before this reader was born. For the reader at that table, almost every line is a surprise. That gap is today's story. The teaching was never lost. It was being read by new eyes. Today's word is rediscovery.
screen: `A PALM LEAF ON A LIBRARY TABLE.` → `OLD WORDS, NEW EYES.` → `NEVER LOST.`

segments.voice: Start with what rediscovery is not. Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand and beyond did not need anyone to find their scriptures. Monks memorized them, copied them and taught them, teacher to student. What changed was who else was reading. As European scholars learned Pali and Sanskrit, they began to translate. Friedrich Max Müller put the Dhammapada into English. Thomas Rhys Davids, who had learned Pali while working in Sri Lanka, turned to the long discourses. He and others formed a society in London to print the Pali texts in Roman letters, so readers who could not read the old scripts could study them. Some of those English versions are the ones this path quotes. Here is a line from Max Müller's Dhammapada: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." An old rule, read again in a new language. The work had its blind spots. Some early scholars treated living Buddhists as if they were footnotes to a dead book. Some Asian Buddhists, including Dharmapala, answered by teaching and publishing for themselves, and the conversation became two-way. And here is the turn: those translations are now old too. Readers today notice their stiff phrasing and their choices of word. So rediscovery keeps happening. Each generation reads the same verses again, checks the old translation, and finds something it missed.
screen: `THE TEACHING WAS NEVER LOST.` · `SCHOLARS LEARN PALI AND TRANSLATE.` · `A SOCIETY PRINTS THE TEXTS.` · `NOW THE TRANSLATIONS ARE OLD TOO.` · then, large: `READ AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line from an old translation. Take today's line: hatred does not cease by hatred; hatred ceases by love; this is an old rule. Say it once, slowly, under your breath. Then settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring the line back on an out-breath. Notice one word that sounds old-fashioned, and one that still lands. You don't have to decide what it means. Just read it again, the way people have for a long time. The bell holds the time.
Rediscovery. The moment Western scholars began reading Buddhist texts that Buddhists had kept alive all along, and the way each generation reads them again. Today's word.
Your line: read again. Today, go back to something you think you already know, a letter, a recipe, a favorite page, and read it once more, slowly. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

pairs: printed Pali texts in Roman letters

Max Müller's Dhammapada and the Rhys Davids translations come from it.

options: stay silent and let them write what they like.
teach and publish for yourself, and join the conversation.

fork.reveal: some Asian Buddhists, Dharmapala among them, taught and published for themselves, and the conversation became two-way.

trapdoor: what you thought: Western scholars discovered Buddhism.
what it means: Buddhists never lost their texts; outside readers began reading them, and every generation reads them again.
what a scholar hears: the Pali texts were printed in Roman letters for new readers, and those Victorian translations are now old enough to be checked and redone themselves.

898.title: The southern map
898.hook: India to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Java
898.howItsDone: Theravada monks in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia chant the Pali texts daily, and monks from these countries have long visited and ordained in one another's monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rediscovery: scholars far away reading texts that Buddhists had kept all along. Your line was read again. What did you go back to? Today, we step back and look at the whole map. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Put your finger on the plain of the Ganges, where the Buddha walked and taught. Now slide it south, down the long coast of India, across a narrow strait to the island of Sri Lanka. From there, swing east across the Bay of Bengal to Myanmar. Keep going into Thailand, up the river to Laos, down into Cambodia, and out across the sea to the island of Java. For many weeks this path has been walking that line one place at a time. Today, the whole southern map at once.
screen: `THE GANGES PLAIN.` → `SOUTH TO THE ISLAND.` → `EAST ACROSS THE BAY.`

segments.voice: First stop, India, where it began, with councils of monks gathering to keep the teaching straight and an emperor, Ashoka, sending messengers outward. Second, Sri Lanka. The island's chronicles say Ashoka's son, the monk Mahinda, brought the teaching there, and a cutting of the Bodhi tree followed. The island became a keeper of the Pali texts. Third, the mainland: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Here the teaching traveled with monks, with traders, and with kings who built and gave. We met Sukhothai's walking Buddhas, the smiling towers of Angkor, and the saffron line at dawn in Luang Prabang. Fourth, the sea road to Java, where Borobudur rose as a mountain of carved stone. Now notice what the map does not show. A line on a map looks like one clean journey. It wasn't. The teaching moved back and forth, over a long time. Monks from the mainland sailed to Sri Lanka to be ordained again, and carried the lineage home. Kings sent for texts and teachers. Some places took up other forms of Buddhism, and some, like Java, later took up other faiths. Today the Theravada tradition, the way of the elders, lives on in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, and its monks chant the same Pali texts. A monk in Colombo and a monk in Vientiane can recite the same verses in the same old language. That shared voice is the southern road.
screen: `INDIA: COUNCILS AND AN EMPEROR.` · `SRI LANKA: MAHINDA AND THE TREE.` · `THE MAINLAND: MONKS, TRADERS, KINGS.` · `THE SEA ROAD TO JAVA.` · then, large: `THE SOUTHERN ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace the southern road on a map. If you have a map or a phone nearby, find India, then Sri Lanka, then follow the coast east. If not, draw it in the air with one finger, slowly. Then let the hand rest and the breath settle. With each breath, name one stop to yourself: India. Sri Lanka. Myanmar. Thailand. Laos. Cambodia. Java. When you reach the end, start again, and let each name be one quiet breath. The bell holds the time.
The southern map. The road the teaching took from India to Sri Lanka and across Southeast Asia, where the way of the elders still chants in Pali. Today's word.
Your line: the southern road. Today, when you travel anywhere, even across town, notice what you carry with you that came from somewhere else. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

original.note: Pali: theravāda, the way of the elders, the form of Buddhism that lives on along the southern road.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism went south once, in a straight line.
what it means: it traveled by monks, traders and kings, and kept moving back and forth.
what a scholar hears: lineages were renewed across the sea, so the southern lands share a Pali canon and keep reviving one another.

899.title: After the Buddha, closed
899.hook: councils, an emperor, an island, a king's questions, a road south
899.howItsDone: Buddhist communities retell the history of the councils, Ashoka and Mahinda at festivals and in sermons, and in Sri Lanka the arrival of Mahinda is remembered each year at the Poson full moon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the southern map, from India to Sri Lanka and across to Java. Your line was the southern road. What did you notice you carry from somewhere else? Today, we close this whole stretch of the story. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

When a teacher dies, the students face a plain question: now what? The Buddha's own last words, in the Pali account, put the work back in their hands. Decay is part of all compound things, he said; keep striving, with care. Then he was gone, and the teaching had no founder in the room. Everything in this part of the path, from the monks gathering to recite to the saffron line in Laos, is the answer to that question. Today, we look back at the whole answer. After the Buddha.
screen: `NOW WHAT?` → `KEEP STRIVING, WITH CARE.` → `THE WHOLE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Five pieces. First, the councils. Monks gathered to recite together what the Buddha had taught, so the words would be kept by many mouths instead of one memory. Later councils argued over the rules, and the community began to divide into schools. Second, an emperor. Ashoka, after a bloody war, carved edicts in stone about restraint and kindness, and sent messengers out from India. Third, an island. In Sri Lanka, the chronicles say, Ashoka's son Mahinda brought the teaching, and the island's monks went on to write the Pali texts down. Fourth, a king's questions. In the Questions of King Milinda, a Greek-born king asks the monk Nagasena hard things: if there is no lasting self, who is talking to me? Nagasena answers with a chariot. Is the chariot the wheels? The axle? The pole? None of them alone, and yet the word chariot works. The king is satisfied, and the conversation goes on. Fifth, the road south: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Java, with monks, traders and kings carrying it from port to port. Put the five together and one thing stands out. The teaching survived by moving. Every time it was recited, written, carved or carried, it reached someone new, and they shaped it too. That is this whole stretch in a sentence: it traveled. Tomorrow it turns north.
screen: `THE COUNCILS RECITE TOGETHER.` · `AN EMPEROR CARVES IN STONE.` · `AN ISLAND WRITES IT DOWN.` · `A KING ASKS ABOUT A CHARIOT.` · then, large: `IT TRAVELED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: retell one piece of this history. Pick one: the monks reciting together, the emperor's stones, the island, the chariot, or the road south. Settle, and tell it to yourself in three plain sentences, as if to a friend who has never heard it. Then let the story go quiet and rest with the breath. If another piece comes to mind, let it pass by like a traveler on the road. The bell holds the time.
After the Buddha. The long stretch when the teaching was recited, argued over, carved, written down and carried across seas, with no founder in the room. Today's word.
Your line: it traveled. Today, tell one person one piece of this story, the chariot or the emperor's stones, and let it travel one step further. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: The Silk Road
900.hook: monks traveled with merchants along the caravan roads into Central Asia and China
900.howItsDone: Buddhist monks have long depended on lay supporters for food and shelter, and merchants and business owners are often among the donors who support monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the southern story: councils, an emperor, an island, a king's questions. Your line was it traveled. Who did you pass a piece of it to? Today a new stretch begins, on the northern roads. Day nine hundred.

Dust, bells and the slow sway of camels. A caravan winds between desert and mountain, loaded with cloth, spices and silver. Walking near the back, in robes the color of the dust, are a few monks. They carry almost nothing: a bowl, a few manuscripts, a teaching memorized by heart. The merchants are glad of them. Monks bless the journey, and some merchants give food and shelter in return. At the oasis towns along the way, small monasteries begin to appear. Today, the northern road opens. The Silk Road.
screen: `A CARAVAN IN THE DUST.` → `MONKS AT THE BACK.` → `MONASTERIES AT THE OASES.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Silk Road is a modern label for a web of caravan routes, not one road, running from the edges of India and Persia, through Central Asia, into China. Goods moved along it, and so did ideas. Second, traders were part of the story from the start. The Vinaya, the monks' rulebook, tells of two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, traveling with a caravan, who met the Buddha soon after his awakening, offered him food, and took refuge in him and his teaching. Traders were in the story before there were monasteries. Third, the oasis towns. Places like Khotan and Kucha, ringed by desert, grew rich on trade, and Buddhist monasteries rose there with merchant money. Monks learned the local languages, and the oases became schools and way stations. The caves carved and painted along these routes still show donors in their best clothes, kneeling beside the Buddha. Fourth, why it worked. A merchant needs trust, a safe night, and a blessing for the road. A monk needs food, company, and a way across the desert. Each gave the other what they lacked. So, as historians tell it, the teaching did not arrive in China by army. Much of it walked in, one caravan at a time, beside the people who were carrying silk the other way. Today's line puts the two together: monks with merchants.
screen: `A WEB OF ROADS, NOT ONE ROAD.` · `TWO MERCHANTS MEET THE BUDDHA.` · `MONASTERIES AT THE OASES.` · `EACH GAVE WHAT THE OTHER LACKED.` · then, large: `MONKS WITH MERCHANTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a caravan. Settle, close the eyes if you like, and let the breath slow to the pace of walking animals. See the line of camels, the bells, the dust. Find the monks near the back. Walk beside them for a while. Each in-breath, a step. Each out-breath, a step. Nowhere to hurry to; the oasis is still far off. If your mind wanders off the road, just come back to the next step. The bell holds the time.
The Silk Road. A web of caravan routes into Central Asia and China, where monks walked beside merchants and the teaching traveled with the trade. Today's word.
Your line: monks with merchants. Today, notice one ordinary trade, a coffee, a delivery, a shop counter, and see what else passes across it besides money. Day nine hundred.

fork.reveal: merchants were often glad of monks: they blessed the journey, and merchants gave food, shelter and money for monasteries.

what a scholar hears: Buddhist monasteries in the oasis towns, funded by trade, became way stations and schools where the teaching was learned and translated on its way to China.

901.title: The first translators
901.hook: An Shigao and others begin translating into Chinese in Luoyang
901.howItsDone: Buddhists in China, Korea and Japan read the sutras in classical Chinese translations, and teachers often explain the translators' word choices when they teach a text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Silk Road, monks walking at the back of the caravans. Your line was monks with merchants. What passed across a counter besides money? Today the monks reach the city, and face a new problem. Day nine hundred one.

How do you say nirvana in a language that has no word for it? That was the job waiting in Luoyang, a great Chinese capital, when monks from the west arrived with texts in their heads and on their backs. The city had readers and writers enough. What it lacked were words. Chinese had no ready words for karma, for rebirth, for a monk's rule. Every sentence was a bridge someone had to build. Today, the people who started building. The first translators.
screen: `NO WORD FOR NIRVANA.` → `A CAPITAL CALLED LUOYANG.` → `EVERY SENTENCE A BRIDGE.`

segments.voice: First, a name: An Shigao. The An in his name marked him, in Chinese records, as coming from Parthia, far to the west. Tradition says he was a prince who gave the throne to an uncle and became a monk. In Luoyang he translated texts on meditation and the breath, on counting breaths and watching the mind. Second, he was not alone. Another monk, Lokakshema, from the Kushan lands, translated some of the early Mahayana sutras. Others joined them. The work was done in teams. A foreign monk recited or read the text, someone turned it into spoken Chinese, and a Chinese scribe wrote it down and polished it. Third, the hard part: the words. Where Chinese had no word, translators sometimes borrowed one from Chinese thought. Some used dao, the way, a word from the Chinese classics, for the Buddhist path. Others sounded the foreign word out in Chinese syllables. Both choices had a cost. A borrowed word brought its old meanings with it, and a sounded-out word meant nothing until someone explained it. Fourth, why it matters. The Chinese Buddhist texts read in China, Korea and Japan today come out of a long line of choices like these, made by people working between languages, at a table, one sentence at a time. Today's line is the direction they faced: into Chinese.
screen: `AN SHIGAO, FROM PARTHIA.` · `TEAMS AT THE TABLE.` · `BORROW A WORD OR SOUND IT OUT.` · `CHOICES STILL READ TODAY.` · then, large: `INTO CHINESE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: translate one idea into your own words. Take a simple teaching about the breath: breathing in, know that you are breathing in; breathing out, know that you are breathing out. Settle, and breathe. Now say it the way you'd say it to a twelve-year-old, or to a friend at the kitchen table. Try two or three versions. Notice what each one gains, and what each one loses. Then let the words go, and rest with the breath, one breath at a time, the way An Shigao's breath texts describe it. The bell holds the time.
The first translators. Monks like An Shigao and Lokakshema, who worked in teams in Luoyang to carry Buddhist texts into Chinese, one choice of word at a time. Today's word.
Your line: into Chinese. Today, when someone uses a word you don't share, a parent, a coworker, a teenager, try putting it into your own words before you answer. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: The White Horse Temple
902.hook: the legend of an emperor's dream and sutras carried on a white horse
902.howItsDone: The White Horse Temple near Luoyang is still an active monastery, and Buddhist pilgrims visit it as a place remembered for the coming of the teaching to China.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first translators in Luoyang, building Chinese words for ideas that had none. Your line was into Chinese. Whose word did you put into your own? Today, the story Chinese Buddhists tell about how it all arrived. Day nine hundred two.

An emperor wakes in the night. In his dream a tall golden figure, shining, flew in front of his palace. In the morning he asks his ministers what it means. One of them has heard of a sage in the far west, called the Buddha, who could rise into the air and whose body shone like gold. The emperor sends envoys west to find out more. That is how the legend begins. It ends with a white horse walking slowly into Luoyang. Today, the White Horse Temple.
screen: `A GOLDEN FIGURE IN A DREAM.` → `A SAGE IN THE WEST.` → `ENVOYS SENT TO FIND HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the dream. The emperor in the story is Ming of the Han, and the golden figure is the spark. The story says he wanted to know, so he sent people to ask. Second, the return. The envoys came back with two monks from the west, and with them came sutras and images, loaded on a white horse. Third, the temple. The emperor had a monastery built for the monks outside Luoyang, and named it for the horse that had carried the teaching: the White Horse Temple. A temple by that name still stands near Luoyang, and Chinese tradition remembers it as the place where the teaching first settled in the land. Tradition says the two monks translated a short sutra there. Fourth, how to hold a legend. Historians read this story carefully. They point out that Buddhists were already in China, among traders and foreigners, before the story's date, and that the account was written down later. So they treat it as a legend, not a record. But a legend tells you something a record can't: how people wanted to remember a beginning. Notice the shape of it. The teaching isn't seized. It isn't preached at the gates. It's asked for, in a dream, and carried in, patiently, by an animal that doesn't know what it carries. The monks walk beside it. That is the picture the legend keeps: the teaching carried in.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S DREAM.` · `MONKS AND SUTRAS ON A WHITE HORSE.` · `A TEMPLE NAMED FOR THE HORSE.` · `A LEGEND, NOT A RECORD.` · then, large: `CARRIED IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the white horse. Settle, and let the breath slow. See the horse standing at the temple gate at the end of the road, dust on its legs, sutras strapped to its back. Watch the monks untie the bundles and lift them down, one by one. Notice the horse's back as the weight comes off. Let each out-breath set something down in the same way, a worry, a task, a tightness in the shoulders. If you like, ask what you are carrying today that might matter to someone else. The bell holds the time.
The White Horse Temple. The monastery near Luoyang named, in the legend, for the horse that carried the sutras into China. Today's word.
Your line: carried in. Today, notice one thing someone carried into your life without making a fuss about it, a habit, a recipe, a kindness, and thank them if you can. Day nine hundred two.

903.title: Kumarajiva
903.hook: the translator who put the Lotus, Diamond and Vimalakirti into Chinese that people still read
903.tomorrow: The tongue that did not burn
903.howItsDone: In Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese temples, Kumarajiva's versions of the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra are chanted in services and studied in classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the White Horse Temple, and the legend of sutras carried into Luoyang on a horse's back. Your line was carried in. What did someone carry into your life? Today, the end of the week, and a translator whose Chinese is still read aloud. Day nine hundred three.

All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, like lightning. That is the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra as it is chanted in Chinese in East Asian temples. The Chinese they chant comes from a translation made in Chang'an, by a team gathered around one monk born in an oasis town on the Silk Road. Quick pictures, each one gone almost as soon as it appears, set down in a Chinese that still sounds clear. His name was Kumarajiva.
screen: `A DREAM, A BUBBLE, DEW, LIGHTNING.` → `CHANTED IN CHINESE.` → `ONE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: First, where he came from. His biography says he was born in Kucha, one of those oasis towns, to a mother from the royal family and a father from India. He became a monk as a boy and studied in Kashmir. He knew the texts, and he came to know Chinese. Second, the long wait. When a Chinese army took Kucha, Kumarajiva was carried off by a general and held for years in a frontier town. It was there, some readers think, that his Chinese grew strong. Third, the work. A later ruler brought him to the capital, Chang'an, and gave him a large team of monks and scholars. Kumarajiva would hold the text, speak it in Chinese, discuss the hard words with the team, and the scribes would write. From that room came the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Vimalakirti Sutra in the versions still chanted and studied. Fourth, his way of translating. His biography tells a story: he said that turning Sanskrit into Chinese is like chewing rice before feeding it to someone. The flavor is lost, and the food may even turn the stomach. He knew what translation costs. Even so, his versions read as clear, flowing Chinese that people could actually say aloud, and some readers credit that clarity for how long they have lasted. Look back at this week: old texts read again, a southern road, a teaching that traveled, monks with merchants, translators at a table, a white horse. And now the translator whose words people still say.
